# 1 Maccabees Chapter 10 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 10 | **Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Council Notes

This chapter is dense political and military history: the rivalry of Alexander Balas and Demetrius I for the Jewish alliance, Jonathan's appointment as high priest, the marriage alliance with Egypt, and Jonathan's military victories. The Demetrius letter (vv.25-45) is a set-piece document — a legal text embedded in narrative, requiring precise rendering of tax and privilege terminology.

**Key term rulings:**
- "Alexander Epiphanes" — the epithet preserved (the author means it ironically, as Alexander Balas was a pretender)
- "purple robe and a golden crown" (v.20) — symbols of royal favor; retained exactly
- "Feast of Tabernacles" (v.21) — preferred over "Feast of Booths" for established English liturgical register
- "salt tax" and "crown levies" (v.29) — technical fiscal terms preserved
- "chief friends" (v.65) — Greek: τῶν πρώτων φίλων; a formal court rank, preserved
- "golden clasp / buckle" (v.89) — Greek πόρπη; "clasp" preferred over "buckle" (more formal)
- Beth-dagon "the temple of their idol" (v.83) — retained; the author's polemical tone is part of the text

---

**1** In the one hundred and sixtieth year Alexander Epiphanes, son of Antiochus, came up and took possession of Ptolemais; they received him, and he reigned there.

**2** When King Demetrius heard of it, he assembled a very large army and marched out to meet him in battle.

**3** Demetrius sent a letter to Jonathan with conciliatory words, designed to honor him.

**4** For he said: "Let us act quickly to make peace with him before he makes peace with Alexander against us,

**5** for he will remember all the wrongs we did to him and to his brothers and to his nation."

**6** He authorized Jonathan to raise troops and furnish weapons, declaring him his ally, and he ordered the hostages in the citadel to be released to him.

**7** Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letters aloud to all the people and to those in the citadel.

**8** They were greatly afraid when they heard that the king had given Jonathan authority to raise an army.

**9** The garrison of the citadel released the hostages to Jonathan, and he returned them to their families.

**10** Jonathan settled in Jerusalem and began to build and restore the city.

**11** He directed those doing the work to build the walls and Mount Zion all around with dressed stone for defense, and they did so.

**12** The foreigners in the strongholds that Bacchides had built took flight;

**13** each man abandoned his post and returned to his own land.

**14** Only in Beth-zur did some of those who had forsaken the law and the commandments remain, for it served as their place of refuge.

**15** King Alexander heard all the promises that Demetrius had sent to Jonathan; he also heard of the battles Jonathan and his brothers had fought and the hardships they had endured.

**16** He said: "Shall we find another man like him? Now let us make him our friend and ally."

**17** He wrote him a letter in these words:

**18** "King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings.

**19** We have heard of you — that you are a man of great valor and deserve to be our friend.

**20** We therefore appoint you today high priest of your nation, and you shall be called the King's Friend — and he sent him a purple robe and a golden crown — and you shall take our side and maintain friendship with us."

**21** Jonathan put on the sacred vestments in the seventh month of the one hundred and sixtieth year, at the Feast of Tabernacles, and he raised troops and equipped them with arms in abundance.

**22** When Demetrius heard these things, he was distressed and said:

**23** "What have we done? Alexander has outmaneuvered us in winning the friendship of the Jews, which gives him their support.

**24** I too will write them words of encouragement and honor and gifts, so that they will stand with me."

**25** He sent them a letter in these words: "King Demetrius to the Jewish nation, greetings.

**26** Since you have honored your agreements with us and remained in our friendship, refusing to side with our enemies, we have heard this and rejoice.

**27** Continue to keep faith with us, and we will reward you generously for all that you do for us.

**28** We will grant you many remissions and will give you gifts.

**29** Now I hereby release you and exempt all the Jews from tribute, from the salt tax, and from the crown levies,

**30** and in place of the one-third of the grain and the one-half of the fruit — which were due to me — I release you from this from today onward and forever. I will not collect them from the land of Judea, nor from the three districts annexed from Samaria and Galilee, from this day and for all time.

**31** Jerusalem and all its territory shall be holy and free from tithe and taxation.

**32** I also surrender my authority over the citadel in Jerusalem and give it to the high priest, to garrison with whatever men he shall select.

**33** Every Jew who has been taken captive from the land of Judea into any part of my kingdom I release without ransom; let all their taxes be cancelled, including the taxes on their livestock.

**34** All feasts, Sabbaths, new moons, and appointed days — and the three days before a feast and the three days after a feast — shall be days of immunity and freedom for all the Jews in my kingdom.

**35** No one shall have authority to exact anything from them or to trouble them in any matter.

**36** Let thirty thousand Jews be enrolled in the royal forces with pay equal to all royal troops; let some of them be stationed in the king's great strongholds,

**37** and let some be appointed to positions of trust in the kingdom. Their officers and leaders shall come from their own ranks, and they shall live by their own laws, as the king has decreed for the land of Judea.

**38** The three districts added to Judea from the region of Samaria shall be incorporated into Judea and counted as one jurisdiction, answerable only to the high priest, not to any other authority.

**39** Ptolemais and its surrounding territory I give as an endowment to the Jerusalem sanctuary for its necessary expenses.

**40** I also give fifteen thousand shekels of silver annually from the royal revenues, from the appropriate accounts.

**41** All arrears that the officials have failed to pay as they did in earlier years shall henceforth be paid to the temple treasury.

**42** Moreover, the five thousand shekels of silver that used to be taken each year from the income of the temple — these are released, for they belong to the priests who minister there.

**43** Anyone who takes refuge in the temple at Jerusalem or within its territory, whatever their debt or obligation — let them be released, and all their property in my kingdom shall be exempt from seizure.

**44** The expense of building and restoring the works of the sanctuary shall be paid from the royal revenues.

**45** The cost of building the walls of Jerusalem and of fortifying it all around, and the cost of building walls in Judea — these too shall be paid from the royal revenues."

**46** When Jonathan and the people heard these words, they put no credence in them and did not accept them, because they remembered the great wrong Demetrius had done in Israel, how severely he had afflicted them.

**47** They were pleased with Alexander, because he had been the first to propose peace, and they remained his allies all his days.

**48** King Alexander assembled a large army and took up position opposite Demetrius.

**49** The two kings engaged in battle; the army of Demetrius fled, and Alexander pursued them and defeated them.

**50** The battle raged until sunset; Demetrius fell that day.

**51** Alexander sent envoys to King Ptolemy of Egypt with this message:

**52** "Since I have returned to my kingdom, taken my seat on the throne of my ancestors, and gained control of the country — for I crushed Demetrius —

**53** I engaged him in battle and he and his army were defeated by us, and we now sit on his royal throne —

**54** let us now establish friendship between us. Give me your daughter as wife; I will be your son-in-law and will give gifts to you and to her worthy of your rank."

**55** King Ptolemy replied: "Happy is the day on which you returned to the land of your fathers and took your seat on the throne of their kingdom.

**56** I will do as you have written. Come to meet me at Ptolemais, so that we may see one another, and I will become your father-in-law as you have said."

**57** Ptolemy set out from Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra and arrived at Ptolemais in the one hundred and sixty-second year.

**58** King Alexander met him, and Ptolemy gave him his daughter Cleopatra in marriage; their wedding was celebrated at Ptolemais with great splendor, as is the custom of kings.

**59** King Alexander wrote to Jonathan, summoning him to meet him.

**60** Jonathan went in state to Ptolemais, met both kings, presented them and their courtiers with silver, gold, and many gifts, and found favor in their eyes.

**61** A group of troublemakers from Israel — lawless men — gathered there to accuse him, but the king paid them no attention.

**62** The king gave orders that Jonathan's clothing be removed and that he be dressed in purple; this was done.

**63** The king seated him at his own side and said to his officers: "Go with him into the center of the city and announce that no one shall bring any charge against him in any matter, and no one shall trouble him for any reason."

**64** When his accusers saw the honor granted him by royal proclamation, and that he was clothed in purple, they all fled.

**65** The king honored him, enrolled him among his chief friends, and appointed him general and governor of the province.

**66** Jonathan returned to Jerusalem in peace and gladness.

**67** In the one hundred and sixty-fifth year Demetrius the son of Demetrius came over from Crete into the land of his ancestors.

**68** When King Alexander heard of it, he was deeply troubled and returned to Antioch.

**69** Demetrius appointed Apollonius as governor of Coele-Syria. Apollonius assembled a large force and encamped at Jamnia, and sent this message to Jonathan the high priest:

**70** "You alone stand up against us, and I have become a laughingstock and a reproach because of you. Why do you exercise authority against us in the hill country?

**71** If you trust your forces, come down to us into the plain and let us try our strength there, for the power of the cities is with me.

**72** Ask and find out who I am and who my allies are; they will tell you that you cannot stand before us, for your ancestors were twice put to flight in their own land.

**73** And now you will not be able to withstand cavalry and such a great force in the plain, where there is no stone, no flint, no place to flee."

**74** When Jonathan heard these words of Apollonius, he was stirred in spirit; he chose ten thousand men, marched out from Jerusalem, and his brother Simon came to his support.

**75** He encamped before Joppa, but the men of the city shut him out, for Apollonius had a garrison there. He attacked it.

**76** The men of the city were frightened and opened the gates; Jonathan took Joppa.

**77** When Apollonius heard, he mustered three thousand cavalry and a large army and marched toward Azotus as if simply passing through, while actually advancing into the plain, trusting in his large cavalry force.

**78** Jonathan pursued him to Azotus, and the armies engaged.

**79** But Apollonius had secretly left one thousand cavalry in their rear.

**80** Jonathan learned there was an ambush behind him; his army was surrounded and pelted with arrows from morning until evening.

**81** The troops held firm as Jonathan had commanded, while the enemy horses grew weary.

**82** Then Simon advanced his force against the phalanx, for the cavalry was exhausted; they broke before him and fled.

**83** The cavalry scattered across the plain, fled to Azotus, and entered Beth-dagon, the temple of their idol, to find safety.

**84** Jonathan burned Azotus and the cities around it and seized their spoils; he burned the temple of Dagon and all who had fled into it.

**85** Those killed in battle together with those burned totaled about eight thousand men.

**86** Jonathan broke camp and marched to Ashkelon; the men of the city came out to meet him with great ceremony.

**87** Jonathan and those with him returned to Jerusalem with rich spoils.

**88** When King Alexander heard these things, he honored Jonathan still more,

**89** and sent him a golden clasp of the kind given to the king's kinsmen, and gave him Ekron and all its territory as a possession.
